title: Jig
pitch: A pattern that reads perfectly can still be impossible to knit. So Jig lets an agent size, chart and re-yarn a whole pattern with you, and refuses any number that will not knit.
about_excerpt: A pattern that reads perfectly can still be impossible to knit. So Jig lets an agent size, chart and re-yarn a whole pattern with you, and refuses any number that will not knit. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration My family's business is yarn. I grew up around patterns covered in red pen, and around customers coming back into the shop a week after buying wool to say the numbers did not work. That is the part people outside the craft do not expect. A knitting pattern can read perfectly and still be impossible to knit. The numbers all have to agree with each other. A cast on has to be a multiple of the stitch repeat plus the edge stitches. A raglan yoke can only reach a target count in whole rounds of eight increases. Shaping has to land on whole rows. Every measurement has to grow as the sizes grow. Break one of those and the pattern still reads like English, prints fine, sells fine, and then fails on somebody's needles after they have paid for the yarn and knitted half a sleeve. Designers do this work in spreadsheets today. A spreadsheet will happily give you a cast on of 87 stitches, because 87 is a number like any other. That is why tech editing is a paid profession and why publishers keep permanent errata pages. So when I read the WebMCP spec, the thing that jumped out was not that an agent could fill in my form faster. It was that the page could say no, and say why. I built Jig for myself first, and I have been grading real patterns in it since. What it does Jig is a knitting design workbench that a person and an agent use at the same time, on the same live document. Ask it for a cast on of 87 stitches on a twelve stitch cable panel. It refuses, names the rule in knitter language, gives back the offending value, and gives back 86 and 98 as the nearest counts that actually fit. The agent reads that one sentence and corrects itself, without ever being told what the repeat was. On the human side those same numbers become one click fixes in the size table. Past that, the agent can do the whole job: read the pattern, read the chart as structured rows rather than a picture, set gauge, grade a full run of sizes while you keep typing into it, swap yarn against a second website and get the answer back in whole skeins, run a tech editing audit, and export. Every call, refusal and correction lands in a transcript in plain English, with whether a person or an agent did it. Why WebMCP fits this use case Three reasons, and all three are about the constraint living in the page instead of behind a server. The rules can refuse. A tool call here is a proposal, not a command. A wrong number comes back with the rule it broke and the nearest values that satisfy it, so the caller never has to work out the arithmetic. It reads one sentence and tries again. That loop is only cheap when the rules sit next to the caller. The rules cannot be bypassed. A person typing, an agent calling a tool, a declarative form submission and the page auditing itself all enter the same propose function. The committed document type carries a private symbol brand, so building one any other way is a compile error. The document is shared rather than handed over. The designer keeps editing while a grading run is in flight, and the run picks up the edit for every size it has not reached yet. There is no session to own and nothing to merge afterwards. What people and agents can do together here that was hard before Correct a refused instruction without ever being told the rule. Ask for 87 and say nothing else. The refusal carries the rule, the offending value, and 86 and 98. A correct second call can only have come from reading that refusal, because the prompt never mentioned the repeat. That is measured against a real browser, not asserted. Edit a number while an agent's grading run is still running. The run reads through a thunk rather than a snapshot, so every size it has not computed yet picks up your keystroke, and neither of you has to wait for the other. Swap yarn across two websites and get a whole skein answer. Change yarn and gauge changes, so yardage per square inch changes, while the new skein has its own length. Two variables at once, which is the classic way to get this wrong. To the agent it is one verb. Underneath it resolves tools on the other origin, invokes them, quarantines every string that crosses the boundary, revalidates through the same gate, and answers in whole skeins per size. Watch the whole negotiation in plain English. Every call, refusal, correction and human edit becomes a sentence in the transcript with its author, so the person is never guessing what the agent just did. How I built it Two real origins, both deployed on Cloudflare Pages. The workbench, and a separate yarn shop site that lends three read only tools to the workbench and to nobody else. The workbench also runs one Pages Function so the model key stays server side and a visitor never needs an API key. Fourteen tools, and deliberately every registration path the spec offers rather than the same one fourteen times: a React hook for the main verbs, raw registration with an AbortSignal for the two tools that only exist while a chart panel is selected, raw registration with exposedTo for the tool named to another origin, and one declarative HTML form that becomes a tool with no registration code at all. The rules live in a pure engine package that cannot import React, the DOM or WebMCP, enforced by a custom lint rule. Every write from every author goes through one propose function, and the committed document type carries a private symbol brand, so building one outside the engine is a compile error rather than a code review note. Sixteen formal correctness properties run over generated inputs with fast-check, including one that proves every repair offered is itself accepted and one that proves no valid value sits between the refused number and the repair. 1,641 tests across 108 files. It also works in a browser with no flag enabled, because a polyfill host stands in and reproduces the real behaviour, refusals included. Challenges I ran into The ones that mattered all came from driving a real browser instead of trusting a test double, and every one of them is now pinned by a test that fails if the fix comes out. An AbortSignal only withdraws a tool when it is the second argument to registerTool . Put it on the descriptor and Chrome accepts it and silently ignores it. executeTool will not take a tool name, it wants the tool object from getTools . Arguments have to be a JSON string, and an object gets rejected. And a refusal's first text part has to stand alone, because some hosts collapse the whole structured result down to content[0].text , so the rule and the repairs have to be in that first part or a model reading only that part gets nothing it can act on. All four of those live in one resolver now, and my fake host reproduces the browser exactly, so a finding cannot quietly regress. My favourite catch was the smallest

live_observation.first_impression: A Sister Mountain article explains grading knitting patterns with a spreadsheet, covering measurements, ease, gauge, formulas, and size calculations. It is an instructional blog page rather than an interactive Jig app.
live_observation.action_attempted: No central app action was available; did not submit newsletter forms or personal data.
live_observation.after_state: The article remained a long-form tutorial with image lightbox controls, cookie controls, and newsletter forms; no pattern-sizing calculator or agent workflow was exposed.
live_observation.notes: The URL is reachable and relevant to pattern grading, but the demonstrated interactive workflow claimed for Jig was not present.
